NEW YORK, Nov 18 : Texas has resumed issuing air permits for data centers, state regulators said on Wednesday, after pausing the practice last month as part of the state's broader attempt to manage the server warehouses and their effects on the electrical grid, communities and the environment. • The Texas Commission on Environmental Quality "has resumed its normal permit review process and will evaluate applications under all applicable state and federal laws and regulations," TCEQ spokesperson Laura Lopez said. • Texas Governor Greg Abbott halted the connection of new data centers to the state electric grid in August and ordered an audit of the projects, rattling one of the world's fastest-growing hubs for data center development. Abbott followed up by temporarily blocking air permits for all data center projects. • The air permit resumption came after the Texas grid operator notified the TCEQ that it had collected "community impact review" information for proposed data center projects, Lopez said.

NEW YORK, Nov 18 : Options on Anthropic shares could begin trading as soon as Monday, giving investors a new way to wager on the AI company's prospects as market participants expect heavy interest. Cboe Global Markets expects to list the contracts two business days after the stock begins trading, pending industry readiness. “The Anthropic IPO could be yet another catalyst, bringing a new wave of investors and trading activity to the options market," said Rob Hocking, Cboe’s global head of derivatives. "It’s great to see investor education driving this growth, as more people learn how options let them define their risk. An exciting trend and one we expect to continue.”  The Claude developer is expected to price its IPO later on Wednesday, and the shares will begin trading on the Nasdaq on Thursday.   "We expect significant interest in Anthropic options once they list," said Garrett DeSimone, head quant at OptionMetrics. "The combination of AI-driven enthusiasm and the lottery-like payoff profile typical of IPOs are likely to draw investors immediately. As one of the most concentrated pure-play exposures to AI, the stock is also likely to be highly volatile."

Nov 18 : While the causes of recent disruptions to the way people work, access bank accounts and travel remain unclear, increased efforts to rapidly patch newly discovered vulnerabilities in the AI age are likely a major factor, according to cybersecurity experts and US officials. US Secretary of State Marco Rubio, speaking to reporters in Manila this week, said company patching efforts are, at times, "creating short-term disruption in the way the system works." Patches are software and operating system updates intended to fix security vulnerabilities found within a program or product. The advent of easily accessible AI tools and large language models has supercharged the discovery of vulnerabilities in software. Microsoft this month has addressed more than 1,200 software vulnerabilities, nearly 20 times higher than in the same month a year ago, according to cybersecurity firm Qualys.

"AI has made finding critical vulnerabilities fast and cheap, and the number of flaws that demand immediate patching has grown with it," said Yuval Itzchakov, CTO and co-founder of autonomous offensive security company A Security.  "Emergency patches go into core infrastructure within hours, often without the full testing cycle, and they are intrusive by design: they change runtimes, kernels and network components that everything else depends on. That speed and scale of change is itself a source of failure," Itzchakov said. Josh Bressers, director of coordinated vulnerability disclosure at cybersecurity firm VulnCheck, said that in 2026 there have been 100,000 publicly disclosed vulnerabilities, tracked by industry as Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures, or CVEs. Of those, Bressers said, 1,363 were known to have been exploited in the real world.  "Given tight resources for defenders, understanding which vulnerabilities need attention first is critical," Bressers wrote in a LinkedIn post. "Not all vulnerabilities are created equal." Anne Neuberger, general partner at Andreessen Horowitz, said that AI is helping attackers find and weaponize vulnerabilities, but is a more "valuable friend" to those tasked with defending key computer networks. "AI is enabling enterprises to find 10 times more vulnerabilities," said Neuberger, who served as deputy national security adviser under former President Joe Biden and led incident response to serious national incidents. "And when patching at scale, some can cause problems."

Nov 18 : "Grand Theft Auto VI" is winning praise from players and critics as it rolls out worldwide, and Wall Street is joining the chorus. Shares of Take-Two Interactive, publisher of the latest edition in the iconic GTA franchise, surged more than 8 per cent on Wednesday as investors bet that glowing initial reviews will fuel demand further and boost the company's bookings and revenue this year. Players waited more than 13 years for GTA VI, and are now doing everything from taking several days of paid time off to signing "contracts" with their partners to get uninterrupted game time. The demand has been feverish. Even with a high bar for player satisfaction, GTA VI saw a flood of early positive reviews and clinched a score of 99 on aggregator site Metacritic.

"The wait appears to have been worth it for gamers and investors alike." Take-Two's stock, down 19 per cent this year through last close, was the top gainer in the Nasdaq-100 index on Wednesday. Wells Fargo analysts raised their estimates for GTA VI sales, projecting about 65 million units in its current fiscal year that runs through March, up from prior projections of 35 million units. The forecast is also underpinned by expectations for a potential PC release early in 2027. The brokerage raised its annual bookings forecast for Take-Two by 19 per cent to $9.76 billion, versus a consensus estimate of $8 billion from LSEG data, and Take-Two's own projection of $8 billion to $8.20 billion. GTA TIDE LIFTS MANY BOATS Another brokerage, Oppenheimer, estimates about $1.85 billion in gross revenue in the first three days, compared with the $1 billion recorded by its predecessor, GTA V, when it was released in 2013. The buzz is expected to lift the broader video game market, with industry researcher Newzoo forecasting 3 per cent growth in the global console player base in 2026, versus a likely decline in the market without GTA VI. "Few releases can change how the whole console market spends, and GTA VI is one of those rare titles," Newzoo's Director of Market Intelligence Emmanuel Rosier said. Analytics firm Sensor Tower estimates the launch will also generate more than 50 million additional visits to food delivery and restaurant apps within 30 days in the US, as gamers hunker down for extended play sessions. Social media apps including YouTube and Reddit are also expected to see greater engagement as fans discuss the game's features and share gameplay clips. Shares of DoorDash rose 2 per cent, while those of Reddit were marginally higher. As of Wednesday noon ET, roughly 17.1 million GTA VI units had been sold, a Sensor Tower tracker showed, far exceeding pre-order volumes of all the biggest game releases in recent history.

NEW YORK/LONDON, Nov 18 : A gauge of global stocks fell in choppy trading on Wednesday after Nvidia's quarterly results and ahead of Anthropic's market debut, while the dollar's strength also weighed on sentiment. The dollar strengthened to a fresh 19-month high after US Federal Reserve Governor Christopher Waller told CNBC the central bank needs to either approve a half-point interest rate hike at its December meeting or communicate a faster pace of hikes in 2027. Mining stocks dragged European shares lower, while Nvidia's results initially helped Asian shares, with Korea's Kospi up 2 per cent overnight. But the Nvidia rally fizzled and the stock was down 2.4 per cent after rising as much as 2.7 per cent. Nvidia's board dismissed the idea of rehiring former CEO Jensen Huang, who resigned last week. The company forecast sales ahead of Wall Street targets on Tuesday.

ROME, Nov 18 : A bid for Italy's Avio by Finnish satellite operator Iceye drew a cool initial response from the Italian government, with the defence minister urging state-controlled Leonardo to "think carefully" before selling its stake in the company. On Tuesday Iceye made a €2 billion ($2.2 billion) cash offer for Avio, with the goal of creating an integrated European space and defence group. Defence and aerospace group Leonardo holds a stake of 18 per cent in the rocket maker. The deal, part of a drive to boost European defence integration and reduce reliance on external providers such as Elon Musk's Starshield, will need a green light from the Italian government under its golden power rules to shield strategic assets. However, it remains to be seen whether and under what conditions Rome would clear the operation, as defence-related groups are seen as key to national interest by Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni, who in the past has imposed tight limits on such deals.

Talking to Reuters ahead of a parliament session in Rome, Defence Minister Guido Crosetto - a key ally of Meloni - said Leonardo should be cautious when considering whether to sell its shares to the state-backed Finnish company. "If I were Leonardo, I would think carefully before exiting (Avio)," he said when asked whether part of the shares should remain in Italian hands to protect national interests. SENSITIVE ASSETS This year, the Italian government allowed equity firms Advent and Nextalia to take over Tinexta group on the condition that its defence arm remained in national hands. It was eventually acquired by state lender CDP. Speaking at an event in Helsinki, Iceye CEO Rafal Modrzewski said the company had held consultations with the parties involved, including governments, before launching the bid, and that it would take a few more months to close the transaction. However, a person close to the matter told Reuters that Rome had not received any formal notification regarding the Avio bid, and said it was therefore unable to assess it. A second official said the government intended to carry out all the necessary steps to assess the transaction and its implications for the national interest. The offer comes at a particularly sensitive moment for Avio, which is building up capacity in the US market through a new manufacturing plant in Virginia, which it expects to complete in late 2028. In contrast with Crosetto's cautious approach, Leonardo CEO Lorenzo Mariani said on Tuesday that he was "pleasantly surprised" by the bid. A source close to Leonardo said that the group had no contact with Iceye before it launched the bid. A second source said Leonardo would soon hold a board meeting to examine the offer. According to a note published on Wednesday by broker Equita, there was a good chance the deal could proceed, with Leonardo eventually retaining a stake to safeguard Italian presence. Avio shares traded 1.5 per cent higher on Wednesday at €39.75, below the €41 offer price. NEW YORK, Nov 18 : Meta’s AI agent Muse, embodied by a smiley, fuzzy mascot named Jolly, has burrowed into encrypted personal messages, supplied made-up information about purchases and sent users chats seemingly meant for other people, a fraught start for a bot meant to simplify life for consumers, according to internal company posts reviewed by Reuters. The unbidden actions by Muse – one of the fastest-growing apps on record, with more than 10 million downloads since its September launch, and the centerpiece of Meta’s plan to generate billions of dollars in AI revenue – have prompted unnerved employees to raise concerns it could be mixing up conversations between different accounts and exposing users’ private data, the posts showed. In some of those cases, Meta staffers reported the agent sending them messages about a childcare request they had not made, career advice they had not sought, product orders they had not placed and bank account balances that were not theirs. In one post, from earlier this month, an employee told colleagues his Muse had randomly added an extra message to its regular chats about fishing-related weather and tide information, saying: “BTW, two bank updates, your Capital One balance is $2722.58, your Charles Schwab balance is $5899.57.”

“I have never shared my bank account with Muse and never discussed any banking topic with Muse. I’m afraid it’s sending other’s bank info to me,” the staffer wrote in his post. In another example, an employee using Muse on her personal phone reported it had surprised her with a reminder to respond to a message from her sister on Signal, an end-to-end encrypted messaging service popular with privacy advocates that competes with Meta’s WhatsApp. “This seems like an extreme privacy violation. I definitely did not grant it access to other apps, or recall being asked about this,” the employee said in her post.  A colleague responded, saying he had discovered Muse was set up by default with permission to access push notifications on phones with Google’s Android operating system after being similarly caught off guard by unsolicited chats related to apps he had not connected. For this story, Reuters reviewed more than two dozen internal posts describing undesired actions by Muse since its debut, many of them from a feedback group where Meta employees flag problems to the team building the agent. Reuters also worked with staff at Signal and the AI Now Institute, a non-profit that studies AI’s impact on society, to replicate Muse’s access to Signal messages. The results of those tests indicated the issue described by the Meta employees was ongoing and could be affecting others. In response to questions about Signal access and other Muse safety concerns, Meta spokesperson Daniel Roberts described the Reuters examples as “isolated incidents,” saying the company prioritizes safety, conducts extensive internal testing and continuously updates products to improve protections. Muse needs to see and interact with people’s computers in order to work on their behalf, and can access other apps only via permissions they explicitly grant, Roberts said. He said many of the messages flagged by employees as potential account mix-ups were hallucinations, a term referring to AI models’ tendency to make things up, and had already been addressed. Reuters was unable to establish whether Muse was giving users other people’s bank account balances and other sensitive data, or making up the information. DEEP ACCESS The Muse incidents highlight the risks associated with an emerging category of consumer AI agents hitting the market from Meta, OpenAI and others, pitched as the next big wave of AI technology. The bots promise to reshape how digital exchanges operate by executing time-saving tasks like answering emails, booking appointments and making online purchases without direct instructions. Meta is ahead of competitors so far, with Muse consistently topping app download charts after heavy promotion to the company’s more than 3.6 billion users on Facebook, Instagram and WhatsApp. The app’s retention rate is also strong, with around a quarter of the people who have set up Muse accounts returning to use it each day, the company has disclosed. To work effectively, agents need deep access to smartphones and computers. However, they are also prone to making mistakes, exploiting obscure loopholes and accomplishing their objectives in sometimes harmful ways. OpenAI and Anthropic, for instance, have revealed instances of their AI agents unexpectedly hacking other companies and weakening systems designed to monitor their activities.  Some banks and retailers have responded to those risks by blocking agents. The technology is also posing new challenges for operating system providers like Apple and Google, which manage the permissions agents use to navigate around people’s devices. Apple, for instance, changed its operating system this week to give people more control over agents’ data usage after an Inc. Magazine columnist accused Muse of reading private chats from the Messages app on his Mac. Meta has assured Muse users it isolates each agent in its own secure “virtual machine” – a cloud-based emulation of a personal computer – and gives people full control over which apps they connect. Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg has cited those protections in dismissing calls for industry-wide AI safety standards, arguing companies already have incentives to build safe products, both to earn consumers’ trust and avoid legal risks. Even so, Meta warns incoming users Muse may make mistakes and its terms of service hold users responsible for the agent’s actions.  REPURPOSING SETTINGS To find out how Muse might access encrypted messages without users’ knowledge, Reuters provided a description of the Meta employee’s post – where the bot randomly prompted her to respond to a Signal message – to staff at Signal and the AI Now Institute. Reuters then worked with them to replicate the access she had observed. Testers prompted Muse to read Signal messages on different operating systems. On an Android phone and an Apple laptop, it responded by bypassing Meta’s “Connector” tool and instead using permissions granted during the bot’s initial setup to pull in the message text, leveraging those authorizations in ways a user might not anticipate. Specifically, on Android, it used its permission to access the device's push notifications to retrieve the messages, just as the Meta employees had described. On Apple’s macOS, it used a combination of the computer’s accessibility and screenshot tools, repurposing settings Apple offers to help people with disabilities operate their computers. The same requests were blocked in tests conducted on an iPhone. The results indicate Meta is interpreting the permissions granted by Muse users broadly, an approach that has long earned the company criticism from privacy advocates and hefty fines from regulators.  In response to Reuters’ findings, Signal President Meredith Whittaker accused Meta of launching Muse “without showing any respect for basic privacy or cybersecurity,” calling the deployment of agents that can gain wide access to people’s devices “technologically reckless.” She called for app developers like Signal to be given “consistent technical ways” to mark their applications as off-limits to AI agents, for Meta and other AI companies to honor those boundaries and for operating system providers to enforce the rules. Presented with the same findings, Apple and Google said they were considering changes to give people more control over what they authorize with AI agents – though Google, like Meta, noted that people already “must deliberately grant permissions” for apps to access Android notifications. Apple said it had built its accessibility tools for people with disabilities and cautioned that leveraging them “for unintended purposes” could put people’s personal information at risk. Its operating system update this week effectively closed the pathway identified by Reuters, sharply restricting developers’ use of accessibility tools on Macs and introducing a new agent-oriented set of permissions.  “We are committed to ensuring users understand exactly what they are allowing, so they can make informed choices about their data and privacy,” Apple said in a statement. ‘NOT MY CONVERSATION’ In other cases discussed internally, staffers reported cases of Muse informing users about transactions that never occurred and making up prices on products they did purchase, costing them real money. In one incident, the agent booked a non-refundable Airbnb stay without permission, an employee reported. Some of the incidents that raised the most concern involved cryptic out-of-context messages sent by the agent that appeared to contain other people’s information, in many cases phrased as replies to queries the users had never submitted.  In a late September social media post, a member of Meta’s Superintelligence team behind Muse initially described a user report of a similar problem as a temporary hallucination-related glitch, resolved the same day it arose. However, the internal posts reviewed by Reuters showed such incidents occurring as far back as mid-September and continuing through this month. In one such post, an employee reported his Muse sending him a message “out of nowhere” saying it was unable to submit a request related to a parent’s control over who could access their child’s data. He had done nothing to trigger the chat, and had never discussed child data or caregiving access with his Muse, he said. When he asked Muse about the message, the bot replied: “I don’t have a good explanation for it other than that it wasn’t related to our conversation. Let’s ignore it. How can I help?” Another staffer said Muse randomly offered to “message the seller” about picking up a coffee table. When the employee asked Muse, “What are you talking about?” the agent responded that it had “pulled in some context about a coffee table pickup that doesn’t seem to be yours.” This was “not my conversation,” the employee said in his post, expressing concern about a “possible cross-account context leak.” To address employee worries, another Superintelligence team member told the internal feedback group in early November that the agent appeared to be hallucinating messages in response to built-in prompts pushing it to engage with users in between sessions. “These (hallucinations) unfortunately bias towards the most uncomfortable topics, like finances/security/safety, which sucks,” he said, adding that he was aware of several other cases involving “crypto-related things too, like giving people updates on their Bitcoin balances.” He said the issues involved both the underlying AI model and the software enabling Muse to take actions, and that the team was working through them. Roberts declined to answer Reuters questions about those issues, including how many there were and why they were persisting.

(Additional reporting by Stephen Nellis and Kenrick Cai in San Francisco; Editing by Anna Driver and Ken Li)

WASHINGTON, Nov 18 : NASA's Voyager 1 probe is believed to have now hit a distance milestone accomplished by no other spacecraft from Earth, based on advance computations by the US space agency, as the probe ventures through the near-emptiness of interstellar space. The robotic probe, launched in 1977, was calculated by NASA to have reached a light-day from Earth, the distance that light travels in 24 hours — about 16 billion miles (26 billion km) — on Wednesday at 5:16 a.m. ET (1016 GMT). Officials at NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory in California will have to wait about a day to get a signal from the probe, confirming it has reached this distance. They have scheduled an event for Thursday to discuss the milestone. "Reaching one light-day is an astounding feat, one that I never expected to see," Voyager project manager Suzanne Dodd said.

Voyager 1, the most distant human-made object, is flying at almost 38,000 miles per hour (61,000 kph). It crossed the outer edge of the heliosphere, a protective bubble of particles and magnetic fields produced by the sun, to enter interstellar space in 2012. Its twin, Voyager 2, was also launched in 1977 and entered interstellar space in 2018. A Jet Propulsion Laboratory representative said recent power-saving measures could give the two Voyager spacecraft enough power to stay in communication with Earth for three to four more years. "But the goal of the mission is to do science, and there is enough power to keep the current suite of instruments going through the 50th launch anniversary next year. Beyond that is hard to predict, and of course these are nearly 50-year-old spacecraft, and there are always things the team cannot anticipate that might happen," the JPL representative said. Voyager 1 journeyed past Jupiter and Saturn, the solar system's two largest planets, earlier in its mission. It continues to gather scientific data. For instance, its instruments have detected the faint monotonous hum caused by the constant vibrations of the small amounts of gas present in interstellar space. "Voyager is sending back continuous measurements of magnetic fields, cosmic rays and of plasma waves that we receive on Earth whenever the Deep Space Network points its antenna at Voyager," Dodd said. The Deep Space Network is NASA's international array of giant radio antennas supporting interplanetary spacecraft missions. "After the heliopause crossing, the magnetic field direction did not rotate into the interstellar direction as expected, but has maintained the direction it had when both Voyagers crossed the heliopause, a direction governed by our sun. We are watching to see when that rotation might occur," Dodd said. "We also are still observing effects from our sun, including strong solar storms like coronal mass ejections, that generate shocks and pressure fronts that reach as far away as Voyager 1 and beyond," Dodd said. "Where does the sun's influence end and pristine interstellar space begin? Perhaps Voyager may last long enough to answer that question."

NEW YORK, Nov 18 : Wall Street, expecting that wealthy investors and retail buyers will battle for shares of Anthropic, is rolling out products tied to the stock, hosting client events and giving away merchandise ahead of the AI company's potentially record launch.  Despite the steep losses among the hyperscalers and other stocks linked to the AI trade in recent weeks, there is building anticipation from these investors for the Anthropic initial public offering, which is expected on Thursday.  The IPO is expected to value the company, which created the Claude chatbot, at up to $1.4 trillion. But it has a hard act to follow after the SpaceX launch, earlier this year, created a frenzy of excitement and events.  "Judging by the number of people interacting with us and asking us about this, and filling out forms, this could be even bigger than SpaceX," said Will Rhind, founder of GraniteShares, who plans to launch a 2x bull Anthropic exchange-traded fund along with a 2x bear product next week.

A successful IPO could boost confidence in other AI-related stocks, including many of the largest technology companies that have powered the stock market rally to a series of record highs, even as shares have recently swung sharply amid questions over the industry's ability to generate measurable profits.  According to industry estimates based on regulatory filings, the market was preparing in coming days for at least 11 leveraged single-stock ETFs from seven issuers, with retail investors accounting for much of the interest.   One advertisement, on the StockTwits investing social media website, read: "Artificial intelligence meets human conviction with the 2X Long Anthropic Daily ETF from Tradr. Coming soon!"  "It’s going to hinge on the bull/bear case for AI," said Rhind. "The believers are not going to be put off by this volatility in the broader AI trade."  Vanda Research, which tracks retail trading activity, said it expects Anthropic itself to attract about $250 million in net retail buying, based on its analysis of activity on listing days and the volume of the company's pre-IPO perpetual futures traded on Hyperliquid. Such a level would double the record $118 million of retail buying for the SpaceX IPO.  Karl Cheong, head of ETFs at Ninepoint Partners in Toronto, points to the selloff in bitcoin and other cryptocurrencies as a sign that retail investors want to raise cash to buy Anthropic. "This will be the first frontier model that retail investors can access easily on a public market," he said. Ninepoint plans to launch an ETF for Canadian investors that would combine leveraged exposure to Anthropic, with a covered call strategy generating income.  WEALTH CLIENTS, LIVESTREAMS, MERCH  Banks have also planned select events. Goldman Sachs organized a launch event on Tuesday for its wealth clients that was attended by the bank's president, John Waldron, as well as Anthropic Chief Financial Officer Krishna Rao and its co-founder and president, Daniela Amodei, according to a person familiar with the matter.  JPMorgan plans to livestream the IPO for clients and has prepared merchandise such as t-shirts and laptop covers, according to another person familiar with the matter. Anthropic Chief Executive Dario Amodei and his team were at the bank's offices all day on Friday meeting investors, the person said. Anthropic declined to comment on the two events. Still, not everyone is jumping on the bandwagon.  London-based Ben Preston, responsible for the Orbis Global Equity Strategy, a long-only stock-picking fund which also has a retail investor base, said the fund will not be buying Anthropic at the IPO. “If it comes in at an IPO value of whatever it is – one and a half trillion dollars – that is a very expensive valuation to pay for a company which is unproven," said Preston.  Although StockTwits users give the anticipated IPO an "extremely bullish" score of 85 out of 100, based on a poll on its site, 67 per cent of the more than 18,000 members who responded said they did not plan to buy Anthropic during the initial offering. Only 20 per cent said they will buy, while another 13 per cent said they would wait to see the price.  Some on social media were skeptical about the potential price of the listing. Others said it has been tougher for ordinary investors to get their hands on pre-IPO shares of Anthropic than for SpaceX shares before the latter's IPO in June.  SpaceX has since had a mixed record, with shares priced at $135 in the IPO, jumping to $150 then briefly as high as $225, before dropping as low as $104. They now trade around $142. Still, "as it has gotten closer to (Anthropic's) launch date, I've seen the excitement and the clamor to get a piece of whatever is allocated to retail grow and grow," said Mitchell Caplan, chairman and CEO of Willow Wealth and former CEO of E-Trade Financial.  OVERSEAS INTEREST  Interest has also been building abroad, with many British platforms inviting retail investors to send orders for shares. “Historically, retail investors have been on the sidelines when it comes to public listings," said Jordan Sinclair, president of Robinhood UK. Yet Susannah Streeter, chief investment strategist at Wealth Club, a British investment platform serving high-net-worth investors, said the IPO highlights the divide between connected buyers who can get in pre-IPO and retail investors who end up pleading with their brokers for part of an allocation.  "It's a bit like arriving at a glamorous launch party – institutional backers on the VIP guest list gain early entry, enjoying the vintage champagne and finest canapés behind closed doors," Streeter said in an email. "By the time the doors finally open to the general public, the risk is that the best of the festivities are well underway and latecomers are left paying a steep entry fee to pick over the flat prosecco and leftover crisps."

KUALA LUMPUR: The global artificial intelligence boom will continue to drive Malaysia’s economy next year, the central bank said on Wednesday, downplaying risks from a potential sector slowdown and tighter scrutiny on data centres. Economic growth surpassed expectations in the third quarter, with gross domestic product rising 5.5 per cent from a year earlier, faster than 5.3 per cent expansions forecast by both a Reuters poll and the government's advance estimates. In September, growth accelerated 6.9 per cent, data from Bank Negara Malaysia (BNM) and the Statistics Department showed. Malaysia's economic performance in the third quarter was underpinned by strong domestic demand, higher investment activities and robust tech exports, according to the data. "Looking ahead, the Malaysian economy is well positioned to build on this momentum in 2027, supported by strong fundamentals and positive outcomes from our structural reform," BNM Governor Abdul Rasheed Ghaffour said, adding that growth was likely to top 5 per cent this year.

The government raised its 2026 growth projections in October, and now expects the economy to expand close to the upper end of a 4.8 per cent to 5.3 per cent forecast range. It expects growth of between 4.2 per cent and 5.2 per cent in 2027. DATA CENTRE INVESTMENTS TO REMAIN 'STRONG' Malaysia has benefited from the AI boom, which has boosted exports of its semiconductors and other tech goods. Net exports rose 5.7 per cent from a year earlier, with shipments of electrical and electronic goods jumping 66.9 per cent, according to Wednesday's data. The country has also attracted billions of dollars in data centre investments, though analysts have warned that growth in the sector could slow following US curbs this week aimed at restricting China's access to advanced AI chips. Abdul Ghaffour said it was too early to assess the impact of the latest restrictions but said data centre investments in Malaysia were expected to remain strong until 2030, based on estimates of ongoing and planned projects. Out of 120 data centre companies, just 13 per cent were Chinese firms, with the rest from the US, Australia, Canada and Malaysia, he said. "It's very well diversified ... while there may be some reaction to (the latest curbs), we believe underlying demand is still strong," he said. While financial market volatility may weigh on AI investments, accelerated AI adoption could boost exports, Abdul Ghaffour said, adding that the tech upcycle will likely "be sustained until next year, although at a more moderate level." BNM SEES 'SPACE' TO MOVE ON RATES BNM kept its benchmark interest rate unchanged for the eighth straight meeting earlier this month. Economists, however, expect the central bank to raise the rate in the first quarter of 2027 amid a resilient economy and rising price pressures. Abdul Ghaffour said headline inflation was expected to edge higher - coming in between 1.5 per cent and 2.5 per cent in 2026 and 1.8 per cent to 2.8 per cent in 2027 - but remain relatively contained. He declined to comment on whether the central bank would hike rates, saying BNM would monitor whether price pressures were building widely and consistently. "If it happens, we have the space, we can be decisive in terms of our actions," he said. Bank Muamalat Malaysia chief economist Mohd Afzanizam Abdul Rashid said Wednesday's data and the current outlook supported the case for a rate increase in 2027. "We foresee the Malaysian economy remaining on a respectable growth trajectory in 2026 and 2027, with the balance of risks fairly even," he said.

Nov 18 : The dollar was pinned at a 19-month high on Wednesday as US economic data and comments from Federal Reserve officials cemented expectations for an interest rate hike next month. Ever since Chairman Kevin Warsh stopped offering markets highly valued forward guidance on the central bank's policy actions, economic data and commentary from influential policymakers have been the strongest source for investors trying to gauge the Fed's next move. Better-than-expected retail sales data on Tuesday on the back of hotter-than-expected inflation data last week have left markets fully pricing a 25-basis-point rate hike in December, and seeing a small chance of a 50-bp rise, the CME Group's FedWatch Tool showed. Influential Fed policymaker, New York's John Williams, said on Tuesday he favoured tighter monetary policy, although he pushed back against the need to shift to a more aggressive path of action.
